title: The finite spectral picture
subtitle: A complete proof of the finite spectral theorem and its projection formulation

slides.title: The finite spectral theorem
slides.lead: Every self-adjoint matrix admits an orthonormal eigenbasis.
body: Self-adjointness is the structural assumption that makes a complete orthogonal decomposition possible. It implies real eigenvalues and preserves the orthogonal complement of each eigendirection.
The result can be stated without fixing a particular eigenbasis: the matrix is a weighted sum of orthogonal projections onto its distinct eigenspaces.
slides.takeaway: The projection formulation is the foundation for studying stable spectral subspaces.

slides.title: Why self-adjointness gives real eigenvalues
slides.lead: Assume A* = A over a finite-dimensional real or complex inner-product space.
body: If Av = λv with v ≠ 0, then ⟨Av, v⟩ equals λ⟨v, v⟩. Self-adjointness makes ⟨Av, v⟩ real because it equals ⟨v, Av⟩, its complex conjugate.
Since ⟨v, v⟩ is positive and real, λ must be real. Distinct eigenvalues likewise produce orthogonal eigenspaces.
slides.formula: Av = λv       A* = A       ⇒       λ ∈ ℝ
slides.takeaway: Real eigenvalues are a consequence of adjoint symmetry, not an extra hypothesis.

slides.title: Find the first eigenvector
slides.lead: Over the complex numbers, the characteristic polynomial always has a root.
body: For a nonzero finite-dimensional complex vector space, det(A − λI) is a polynomial of positive degree. The fundamental theorem of algebra supplies a root λ.
At such a root, A − λI is singular, so its kernel contains a nonzero eigenvector v. Normalize v to unit length. The rest of the argument finds eigenvectors perpendicular to v.
slides.takeaway: The existence step is finite-dimensional and uses complex algebra.

slides.title: The key invariant complement
slides.lead: Let v be a unit eigenvector of a self-adjoint operator A.
body: Take any w orthogonal to v. Moving A across the inner product gives ⟨Aw, v⟩ = ⟨w, Av⟩. Substituting Av = λv yields zero. Thus Aw is also orthogonal to v.
The space splits into the line through v and the perpendicular subspace v⊥. Both are invariant, and the restriction to v⊥ remains self-adjoint.
slides.takeaway: Invariant orthogonal complements make the spectral theorem induction possible.

slides.title: Complete the proof by induction
slides.lead: The restriction to v⊥ is a smaller self-adjoint problem.
body: In dimension one, the conclusion is immediate. For dimension n, choose a unit eigenvector v. The orthogonal complement has dimension n − 1, is invariant, and carries a self-adjoint restriction.
By induction, v⊥ has an orthonormal eigenbasis. Add v. The resulting list is orthonormal, consists entirely of eigenvectors of A, and spans the full space.
slides.takeaway: Existence → invariant complement → induction → complete orthonormal basis.

slides.title: The real symmetric case
slides.lead: Complex diagonalization does not force us to use complex eigenvectors for a real matrix.
body: Regard a real symmetric matrix as complex Hermitian and obtain an eigenpair (λ, z). Its eigenvalue λ is real. Write z = x + iy, where x and y are real vectors.
Because A and λ are real, Ax = λx and Ay = λy. At least one of x or y is nonzero. This yields a real eigenvector; the same orthogonal-complement induction works over ℝ.
slides.formula: A(x + iy) = λ(x + iy)  ⇒  Ax = λx,  Ay = λy
slides.takeaway: Every real symmetric matrix has a real orthonormal eigenbasis.

slides.title: Group equal eigenvalues into eigenspaces
slides.lead: Eigenvectors of a repeated eigenvalue are not individually canonical.
body: For each distinct eigenvalue λ, define Eλ = ker(A − λI). These eigenspaces are pairwise orthogonal. Their orthogonal direct sum fills the full space.
Write Pλ for the orthogonal projection onto Eλ. This projection is uniquely determined by A and λ, regardless of the basis chosen inside the eigenspace.
slides.formula: Eλ = ker(A − λI)       Pλ² = Pλ = Pλ*
slides.takeaway: A spectral projector identifies a whole eigenspace, not a chosen set of eigenvectors.

slides.title: The spectral decomposition
slides.lead: Spectral projections resolve the identity and reconstruct the operator.
body: Projections onto different eigenspaces annihilate one another. Their sum is the identity because every vector splits uniquely into eigenspace components.

Applying A scales each component by its eigenvalue. Therefore A equals the sum of λPλ over distinct eigenvalues. More generally, any polynomial in A acts by the corresponding polynomial on each eigenspace.
slides.formula: Σλ Pλ = I      PλPμ = 0 (λ ≠ μ)      A = Σλ λPλ
slides.takeaway: Spectral decomposition is coordinate-free once the eigenspace projectors are identified.

slides.title: Example: a symmetric 2 × 2 matrix
slides.lead: Consider A with diagonal entries 2 and off-diagonal entries 1.
body: The vector (1, 1) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 3. The perpendicular vector (1, −1) has eigenvalue 1. After dividing both by √2, they form an orthonormal basis.
The corresponding projectors have entries ±½. The next slide checks their identities and reconstructs A explicitly.
slides.takeaway: Diagonalization exposes two independent modes with distinct eigenvalues.

slides.title: Verify the projections exactly
slides.lead: The spectral theorem can be checked using two small matrices.
body: Projecting onto the line through (1, 1) gives P₃, whose entries are all one half. Projecting onto (1, −1) gives P₁, with positive diagonal and negative off-diagonal entries.
Their sum is I. Weighting them by their eigenvalues reproduces A. No approximation or choice of a privileged coordinate system is involved.
slides.takeaway: The identity is an operator identity, verified by ordinary matrix multiplication.

slides.title: Repeated eigenvalues and selected clusters
slides.lead: The projector is stable under a change of basis inside an eigenspace.
body: Suppose λ has a two-dimensional eigenspace. Every orthonormal pair spanning it produces the same projection Pλ. Rotating the pair changes their coordinates but not the subspace.
For a selected set S of eigenvalues, add the corresponding projections. This produces the spectral projection onto the whole cluster; perturbation theory measures how that selected subspace changes.
slides.formula: Pₛ = Σ(λ∈S) Pλ      Pₛ² = Pₛ = Pₛ*
slides.takeaway: Clusters and their projections are the natural objects for Davis–Kahan bounds.

slides.title: Why the assumptions matter
slides.lead: A general square matrix need not possess an eigenbasis.
body: For example, the matrix [[1, 1], [0, 1]] has only one independent eigenvector. It cannot be diagonalized using any basis, let alone an orthonormal one.
Likewise, an infinite-dimensional bounded self-adjoint operator may have continuous spectrum without an eigenbasis. Spectral integrals replace finite sums in that setting.
slides.formula: [[1,1],[0,1]] has eigenvalue 1 but only a one-dimensional eigenspace
slides.takeaway: The finite theorem assumes self-adjointness and finite dimension.

slides.title: A proof you can reconstruct
slides.lead: The mathematical argument has four reusable steps.
body: First obtain an eigenvector from the characteristic polynomial. Second prove its eigenvalue is real. Third establish invariance and self-adjointness of the perpendicular complement. Fourth apply induction and collect the projections.
The same decomposition allows finite functional calculus: for any function defined on the finite spectrum, set f(A) = Σ f(λ)Pλ.
slides.takeaway: A = Σ λPλ is the finite spectral picture used throughout subspace perturbation theory.
